forces: Two violins, two violas and two cellos
performers: Hollywood String Quartet (Felix Slatkin and Paul Shure, violins; Paul Robyn, viola; Eleanor Aller, cello); Alvin Dinkin, viola; Kurt Reher, cello
intro: The Hollywood String Quartet and two guests play the original six-string version of Verklärte Nacht, Op. 4, in which two people walk through a cold wood and the woman tells her companion she is carrying another man’s child. The LP’s first side (bars 1–228) ends before his answer.

sections.label: A · Low strings, descending phrase
sections.mNote: A descending phrase above repeated low notes

sections.label: B · The woman’s confession, string sextet
sections.mNote: The six strings play the music of the woman’s confession.

sections.label: C · Violin melody in E major
sections.mNote: Long violin phrases over moving viola and cello parts

sections.label: D · The walk after the confession
sections.mNote: The woman waits for her companion’s answer.

sections.label: Link · E♭ minor, low B♭ held
sections.mNote: The second cello holds a low B♭ into side two.

cues.title: Opening, violas and cellos
cues.text: The second viola and second cello repeat a low D. Above them, the first viola and first cello begin a descending phrase marked immer leise (always quiet). The violins rest until later.
cues.evidence: Original sextet score, Dreililien-Verlag, plate 345 (1905), p. 3, bars 1–9, composer’s copy at the Arnold Schönberg Center. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/manuskripte.php?werke_id=420&id_quelle=1213&herkunft=allewerke
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dehmel’s poem, the woman’s confession
cues.text: Richard Dehmel’s poem places two people beneath bare trees and a bright moon. The woman speaks first: “Ich trag ein Kind, und nit von Dir” — “I carry a child, and it is not yours.” Her companion has not yet replied.
cues.evidence: Dehmel, Verklärte Nacht, Weib und Welt (1896), reproduced on p. 2 of the sextet score (Dreililien-Verlag, 1905). Translation ours. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/manuskripte.php?werke_id=420&id_quelle=1213&herkunft=allewerke

cues.title: Payerbach, September 1899
cues.text: In September 1899 Schoenberg spent a holiday in Payerbach with Alexander Zemlinsky and Zemlinsky’s sister Mathilde, who later became Schoenberg’s wife. He composed Verklärte Nacht there in three weeks. The finished manuscript is dated 1 December.
cues.evidence: Therese Muxeneder, Arnold Schönberg Center work essay: Payerbach holiday, three-week composition and final manuscript date. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: Schoenberg’s announcement, 1902
cues.text: In 1902 Schoenberg explained his aim of bringing the poetic programme of orchestral music into chamber music. No singer takes the parts of Dehmel’s speakers. Two violins, two violas and two cellos carry the whole story.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s announcement in Deutsche Tonkünstler-Zeitung, 21 October 1902, reproduced by the Arnold Schönberg Center. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: First violin theme in E major
cues.text: The music moves to E major, marked Etwas ruhiger (a little calmer). The first violin plays the melody over moving figures in the second viola and first cello. In Schoenberg’s account of the poem, this theme belongs to the woman’s longing for motherhood.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 12–13; Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), fourth theme, example 7. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: End of the woman’s confession
cues.text: The woman’s confession is over. In Dehmel’s poem she walks awkwardly beside the man she loves and looks up at the moon. His reply begins by lifting the burden from her unborn child.
cues.evidence: Dehmel, Verklärte Nacht (1896), third and fourth stanzas, reproduced in the original sextet score, p. 2; Schoenberg’s 1950 commentary places this scene before the D-major answer. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: E♭-minor ending, low B♭
cues.text: The strings settle in E♭ minor and stop until only a low B♭ remains in the second cello. The first side of the LP ends on that note, at bars 228–229. Side two opens in D major.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 24–26, bars 204–229; Schoenberg’s 1950 commentary explains the E♭-minor ending and its connecting B♭. The LP division is at bars 228–229. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A violin melody in E major
transitions.from: B · The woman’s confession, string sextet
transitions.to: C · Violin melody in E major
transitions.how: The sextet broadens at Breiter and moves into the E-major episode. At Etwas ruhiger the first violin plays the long melody, with the second viola and first cello moving beneath it and the second cello playing the slower bass line.
transitions.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 12–13, and Schoenberg’s 1950 programme notes, example 7. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

transitions.title: Second cello’s held B♭, end of side one
transitions.from: D · The walk after the confession
transitions.to: Link · E♭ minor, low B♭ held
transitions.how: Over E♭ minor the upper strings thin out and stop. The second cello continues to hold B♭ after the other parts have stopped. That B♭ connects the first half to the broad D-major section on the next side.
transitions.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 24–26, bars 204–229; Schoenberg’s 1950 programme notes, examples 9–10. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

source.locator: Pages 3, 12–13 and 24–25, bars 1–228. Two violins, two violas and two cellos; the two viola parts and the two cello parts are grouped together here.

timeline.note: First viola and first cello descend over the low D repeated by their partners.
Both violins join the descending phrases of the violas and cellos.
All six strings play, passing melodic phrases between the upper and lower instruments.
The first violin plays in E major above moving second viola and first cello.
The sextet returns to the walking music after the woman’s confession.
The upper strings stop over E♭ minor, leaving a low B♭ in the second cello.

composer.epithet: Composer who abandoned tonality, continued to study Bach and Brahms, and wrote a minuet using all twelve notes.
facts: Largely self-taught; lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky
Alban Berg and Anton Webern from 1904; later Hanns Eisler and John Cage
Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33; UCLA, 1936–44
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
At the première of Pierrot lunaire in Berlin on 16 October 1912, Albertine Zehme stood onstage in a Pierrot costume. Behind a screen, five instrumentalists watched Arnold Schoenberg conduct. They had held twenty-five ensemble rehearsals to prepare thirty-odd minutes of music in which the voice slid away from its written notes, the flautist also played piccolo and the violinist also played viola.

Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt in 1874 and began learning the violin as a child. His father died when he was fifteen. From 1891 to 1895 he worked in a bank, making music with friends and teaching himself from scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him lessons. From Brahms he learnt how a small phrase could grow through continual change, and from Wagner how long the resolution of a chord could be delayed.
